objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how unusual attitudes are prevented and recovered from by instruments, set one up safely for a learner, demonstrate nose-high and nose-low recoveries from the right seat while explaining them, and spot and fix a learner's assessment and control errors.
why: Loss of control in flight is the leading cause of fatal general aviation accidents [[24:106|AFH 5-1]], and continued VFR into IMC and instrument failure are named LOC-I scenarios [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]. Every private pilot applicant must be trained in recovery from unusual flight attitudes by reference to instruments [[60:300|14 CFR 61.109(a)(3)]], often by a new CFI. The few recoveries you teach are what that pilot will have on the night the horizon disappears.

prereading.label: IFH 7-55 to 7-60

warmup: Think first: your instrument student nails every recovery when you say "recover" after she has had her eyes closed for 20 seconds. Last week, though, she lost 400 feet in a descending turn while loading an approach, and did not notice until the altimeter warning chimed. What did your eyes-closed drills teach her, what did they leave out, and how would you change the next lesson?

key_terms.def: An unintentional, unanticipated, or extreme aircraft attitude [[1:508|PHAK G-32]]; one not normally required for instrument flight [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].
An event that unintentionally exceeds normal flight or training parameters: pitch over 25° nose up, over 10° nose down, bank over 45°, or a wrong airspeed for the conditions [[24:106|AFH 5-1]].
Loss of control in flight: any significant deviation of an aircraft from the intended flightpath, often from an upset [[24:106|AFH 5-1]].
Upset prevention and recovery training; it should include slow flight, stalls, spins and unusual attitudes [[24:106|AFH 5-1]].
Timely use of the flight controls and thrust, in proportion to the excursion, to stop a developing upset before it becomes fully developed [[24:111|AFH 5-6]].
An uncontrollable, automatic muscle reflex with raised heart rate and blood pressure, set off by a sudden, intense event [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].
Lack of orientation with regard to the position, attitude, or movement of the airplane in space [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]].
Forward elevator pressure to bring the airplane back to about +1 G, reducing AOA and G-load before rolling level [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].
Flight with the attitude and heading indicators covered or inoperative; all IFH analog maneuvers except the instrument takeoff can be flown this way [[23:162|IFH 7-1]].
PFD software, fed by the AHRS, that shows red chevrons pointing back to the horizon and declutters the display in extreme attitudes [[23:216|IFH 7-55]] [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].
A PFD indication showing where airspeed and altitude will be in 6 seconds [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].
A turn made to be sure the next maneuver will not proceed into another aircraft's flightpath [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

Resources: aircraft versus aircraft or a full-flight simulator.

chunks.title: What you are really teaching, and where it fits

body.p: An unusual attitude is an airplane attitude not normally required for instrument flight. Outside training it is never intentional, so it comes as a surprise, and an untrained pilot reacts by instinct with abrupt, purposeless muscle effort [[23:187|IFH 7-26]] [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. Your job is to replace that instinct with a cross-check and a fixed sequence.

The stakes are plain. LOC-I tops the FAA list of causes of fatal general aviation accidents, and unintended flight into IMC is on the same list [[30:21|RMH 3-3]]. The RMH names continued VFR into IMC, wake turbulence, thunderstorms, instrument failure and loss of outside references at night or over water as LOC-I scenarios [[30:22|RMH 3-4]].

head: Who you teach
What the rule requires
rows: Private pilot learner
3 hours by reference to instruments that include recovery from unusual flight attitudes [[60:300|14 CFR 61.109(a)(3)]]
Commercial pilot learner
10 hours of instrument training with a view-limiting device that include partial panel skills and recovery from unusual flight attitudes [[60:314|14 CFR 61.129(a)(3)(i)]]
Instrument student
The IFH sample syllabus puts partial panel operations in Lesson 6 and recovery from unusual attitudes, with partial panel practice, in Lesson 7 [[23:343|IFH B-2]]

body.p: **Unusual attitude or upset?** The AFH draws a line. An upset has defined limits, includes stalls and wrong airspeeds, and centers on surprise. A 30° bank with the nose 15° up that an instructor sets up is an unusual attitude, not an upset [[24:106|AFH 5-1]] [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. Most of what you fly with a learner is the first; what you are preparing them for is the second.

callout.text: The learner side of this Task is covered in the Private (PA.VIII.E) and Instrument (IR.IV.B) lessons: the recognition table, illusions, spiral dive and load factor. This lesson adds the instructor's view: prevention you can teach, how to set attitudes up safely, and how to read a learner's mistakes.

check.q: Which sample IFH syllabus lesson comes right before recovery from unusual attitudes, and why does that order make sense?
check.a: Lesson 6, partial panel operations [[23:343|IFH B-2]]. The recovery starts from the airspeed indicator, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator when the POH gives no procedure [[23:188|IFH 7-27]], so the learner needs those skills first.

body.p: K1 names four groups of factors. Teach each by name, with a prevention habit the learner can practice today.

head: Factor
What the sources list
Prevention to teach
rows: Flight causal factors

Turbulence, disorientation, instrument failure, confusion, preoccupation with flight deck duties, careless cross-checking, misreading instruments, weak aircraft control [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]; poor trim and a disorganized flight deck [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]
Keep the airplane trimmed for level flight at all times, arrange items for easy access, and never stop the cross-check for a head-down task [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]
Physiological factors

Illness, medication, alcohol, fatigue, sleep loss and mild hypoxia raise susceptibility to spatial disorientation [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[23:76|IFH 3-9]]; rotational acceleration of 2° per second or lower is below the inner ear's detection threshold [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]
Be physically tuned for reduced visibility, avoid sudden head movement, and trust the instruments over sensations [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[23:76|IFH 3-9]]
Environmental factors

Turbulence such as clear air turbulence, mountain waves, wind shear, thunderstorms and microbursts, plus wake turbulence and icing [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. Night and weather that hide the natural horizon raise the risk of spatial disorientation (the AFH files continued VFR into IMC under human factors) [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]
A full weather briefing; training and proficiency before flying in visibility under 3 miles or with no visible horizon [[23:75|IFH 3-8]]
System and equipment failures
Asymmetric flaps, binding controls, runaway trim, autoflight malfunction [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]; vacuum pump failure, forgotten pitot heat [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]
Know systems and POH/AFM procedures; stay proficient on secondary instruments and partial panel [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]

body.p: **A case to teach from.** The AIH and RMH both use an accident in which the vacuum pump failed in VMC and the pilot continued into IMC instead of diverting. The failed instruments were an aircraft hazard, the IMC an environment hazard, and together they made the risk unacceptable [[25:186|AIH 10-2]] [[30:11|RMH 1-2]]. The AIH says the most effective fix may have been a decision, not a flying skill: divert and land while still in VMC [[25:186|AIH 10-2]].

callout.text: Four doors into an unusual attitude: the flying (causal), the body (physiological), the sky (environmental), the machine (systems). Ask the learner which door each scenario walks through.

check.q: A learner forgets pitot heat in IMC and later loses control on partial panel. Which K1 groups are at work?
check.a: A system and equipment failure that leads to extended, unpracticed partial panel flight, which the AFH lists under task saturation [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]; IMC adds an environmental factor [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].

chunks.title: How LOC-I builds: stress, saturation, scan and disorientation

body.p: R1 lists stress, task saturation, an inadequate scan and spatial disorientation. In the airplane they rarely come alone, so teach them as a chain.

bullets: **Stress and startle.** Untrained pilots often meet an upset with surprise or a startle response [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. The AIH notes that anxious learners may freeze, or act without rational thought [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].
**Task saturation.** When task requirements exceed pilot capability the margin of safety is gone; extended, unpracticed partial panel flight at night is the AFH example [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

**Task prioritization.** Separating time-critical information from distractions takes practice and knowledge of the airplane. Cross-checks confirm what is shown and catch information that is missing or invalid, such as a failed stall warning [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

**Inadequate scan and distraction.** Many upsets happen while the pilot is busy with a task that takes attention away from the instruments [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. Setting avionics while hand flying is enough [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].
**Spatial disorientation.** Disoriented pilots may not know it. The AFH calls this unrecognized disorientation, the kind where no corrective action is taken [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

**Loss of situational awareness.** Distractions, unexpected events, high workload and inoperative equipment reduce it; a pneumatic failure that takes the attitude and heading indicators can leave a pilot in an unusual attitude [[23:337|IFH 11-12]].

body.p: **Show, don't tell.** The IFH and PHAK give in-flight demonstrations: with the learner's eyes closed, you accelerate in level flight (it feels like a climb), or roll slowly into a coordinated turn of about 50° (it also feels like a climb) [[23:75|IFH 3-8]]. Even no sensation at all is a lesson, because it shows the body cannot detect the bank [[23:74|IFH 3-7]]. Never do them at low altitude or without an instructor or safety pilot [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].

callout.text: The rolling-beyond-the-vertical demonstration can produce intense disorientation: with the learner's eyes closed or gaze lowered to the floor, you start a positive, coordinated roll toward 30° to 40° of bank while the learner tilts the head forward, looks to one side, then brings the head upright [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]]. Time it so the roll stops as the head comes upright [[23:75|IFH 3-8]]. Application: save it for after the gentler demonstrations.

check.q: Why is "no sensation at all" a useful result in a disorientation demonstration?
check.a: It shows the learner cannot detect bank or roll, which is the point of the demonstration [[23:74|IFH 3-7]].

body.p: The first thing the learner does is not move the controls. It is to recognize that something is wrong and to identify what. The rule: any instrument rate or indication that does not fit the maneuver being flown means assume an unusual attitude and speed up the cross-check, to confirm the attitude, an instrument error or an instrument failure [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[24:110|AFH 5-5]].

**Teach the order of reading.** Airspeed tells pitch direction: decreasing or below the desired value is nose-high, increasing or above it is nose-low [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. The altimeter and VSI confirm it, and the attitude indicator and turn coordinator give bank, with the ball showing coordination [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. The attitude indicator is the quickest picture, except in extreme attitudes [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].

head: Instrument limit
What to teach
rows: Spillable attitude indicator
May have passed its limits or failed; do not depend on it [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
Nonspillable, working
Errors up to 5° in pitch and bank; very hard to read in extreme attitudes [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
Pitch-limited gyro (some models)
May peg or tumble and give wrong pitch and bank, which can confuse an unusual attitude recovery [[1:221|PHAK 8-19]]
Glass attitude display
Keeps some sky and some ground in view; the horizon line starts moving down at about 47° nose-up and up at about 27° nose-down [[23:216|IFH 7-55]]
Glass horizon reference
The white line is the horizon; the blue-brown break is only a reference [[23:216|IFH 7-55]]

body.p: **Interpreting is a skill you can test.** Before the hood goes on, show the learner Figure 7-39 and Figure 7-40 and ask for the attitude out loud, instrument by instrument. On a PFD, the trend vectors show where airspeed and altitude will be in 6 seconds, and the heading trend shows which way the airplane is turning [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

callout.text: Incorrect assessment of the type of upset tops the AFH list of recovery errors [[24:112|AFH 5-7]]. A learner who pushes forward because the nose "feels" high, without reading airspeed, has skipped assessment.

check.q: Airspeed is above the desired value and climbing. Before any other reading, what does that tell the learner?
check.a: The nose is low; increasing airspeed means a nose-low attitude [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

body.p: Use the POH/AFM procedure if there is one. If not, recover by reference to the airspeed indicator, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. For a nose-high attitude (airspeed decreasing or below the desired value) the IFH gives this order, with the inputs made almost at the same time [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]:

head: Step
Control
What you say while you demonstrate
rows: Increase power, in proportion to the observed deceleration [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
"Airspeed is dropping, so power comes up first, more if it is dropping fast."
Forward elevator pressure to lower the nose and prevent a stall [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
"Nose down, not to a dive, just enough to stop the airspeed loss."
Coordinated aileron and rudder to level the miniature aircraft and center the ball [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
"Wings level on the turn coordinator, ball centered."
Level pitch confirmed when the airspeed and altimeter needles reverse and stabilize [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
"Altimeter stopped, airspeed stopped. That's level."
Straight, coordinated flight confirmed by a level miniature aircraft and a centered ball [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
"Now I add the attitude indicator back in."
Return to the altitude you or ATC assigned once stable [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
"Back to 4,500, at a normal rate."

body.p: **When the nose-high attitude has become a stall.** If the stall warning or buffet is already there, the AFH stall recovery applies: reduce the AOA first, then roll level, then add power. Power reduces altitude loss but does not end a stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Teach the learner that the airspeed and the stall cues decide which picture they are in.

callout.text: To return to the assigned altitude, the IFH rule of thumb is a vertical speed double the altitude error, never more than the airplane's optimum rate, which varies from 500 to 1,000 fpm [[23:197|IFH 7-36]] [[23:198|IFH 7-37]]. More than 200 fpm beyond the rate wanted is overcontrolling [[23:198|IFH 7-37]].

check.q: Without the attitude indicator, how does the learner know pitch is level in a nose-high recovery?
check.a: The airspeed and altimeter needles reverse direction and stabilize [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

body.p: For a nose-low attitude (airspeed increasing or above the desired value), the IFH order is different, and the difference is the lesson [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]:

bullets: 1. **Power:** reduce power to prevent excessive airspeed and altitude loss [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

2. **Bank:** correct to straight flight with coordinated aileron and rudder, by the turn coordinator, with the ball centered; slips and skids can aggravate disorientation and slow the recovery [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].
3. **Pitch:** raise the nose to level with smooth back elevator pressure [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

4. **Watch for overcontrol:** keep a fast cross-check, since the first pressures may be large. Needles slowing means nearing level; needles stopping and reversing means passing through level [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].
5. **Add the attitude indicator** once the airspeed, altimeter and turn coordinator stabilize, then return to the assigned altitude [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

body.p: **By the numbers first.** All controls can be changed at once in a smooth, proficient recovery, but in initial training the IFH wants a positive recovery made by the numbers in that order [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. Blend them later, when the order is automatic.

**Why bank before pitch.** The instinctive reaction to a nose-down attitude is to pull back [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. In a steep, nose-low spiral, a startled pilot who pulls while rolling level can create loads that damage or break the airframe [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. That is control input error R3 in its most dangerous form; the full five-step spiral dive recovery is in IR.IV.B and AFH 5-26.

**The AFH template is not the IFH order.** For upsets in general the AFH gives: disconnect the autopilot, unload, roll to the nearest horizon, adjust power by monitoring airspeed, return to level flight, and it says to follow the AFM/POH procedure first [[24:111|AFH 5-6]]. Teach one sequence per learner and say which source it comes from.

check.q: Your learner raises the nose before leveling the wings in a nose-low recovery. What does the IFH order say, and what is the hazard?
check.a: Bank comes before pitch: power, bank, then pitch [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. Pulling while banked or rolling can overload the airframe in a spiral [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

body.p: The IFH recovery is already a partial panel recovery: with no POH procedure it starts from the airspeed indicator, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. All the IFH analog maneuvers except the instrument takeoff can be flown with the attitude and heading indicators covered or inoperative [[23:162|IFH 7-1]], so teach recoveries both ways.

**Why it matters.** A vacuum failure lets the gyros slow and wander. A pilot who misses the off flags can turn a benign failure into a dangerous unusual attitude that needs a partial panel recovery, and many small airplanes have no vacuum warning, so the vacuum gauge must be in the scan [[23:332|IFH 11-7]] [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

bullets: **Spot it:** a warning flag, or an attitude indicator that disagrees with the supporting instruments; compare it right away with the turn indicator and VSI [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].
**Fly it:** use the instruments that still work; covering the failed ones may help, then advise ATC and declare an emergency if needed [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

**Pitch on partial panel:** the altimeter is the primary pitch reference; first stop the needle with a smooth input, then change pitch to go back. Abrupt yoke inputs cause large pitch changes and an oscillation that compounds the deviation [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].

body.p: **Glass panel failures.** If the AHRS fails, all unusual attitude protection is lost along with attitude and heading on the PFD [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. In the IFH example airplane only the altimeter and VSI tape then show a nose-high attitude, the slip/skid indicator is gone, and there is no standby turn coordinator [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. With AHRS and air data both failed, the standby airspeed, attitude indicator, altimeter and compass are all that remain [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

callout.text: Teach the learner to say what failed before fixing anything: "Attitude fail, I'm on standby attitude and the altitude tape." Then recover by the same IFH order with what is left.

check.q: Your learner's attitude indicator shows a bank the other instruments do not agree with. Which quick comparison does the IFH give to find the failed part?
check.a: Compare the attitude indicator right away with the rate-of-turn indicator and the VSI; this checks the vacuum or pressure gyro against the electric and static instruments [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

chunks.title: The operating envelope and control input errors

body.p: A recovery is not finished when the wings are level. It is finished when the airplane is level without being stalled or overstressed. The AFH says recovery inputs should be in direct proportion to the amount and rate of roll, yaw, pitch or airspeed change, to avoid overstressing the airplane, unless ground contact is imminent [[24:109|AFH 5-4]].

head: Envelope fact
Why it matters in a recovery
rows: Load factor in a level, coordinated 60° bank is 2 G; at 80° it is 5.76 G [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]
Pulling in a steep bank piles on G fast
Normal category limit load factor is 3.8 to -1.52 [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]
Little margin for a rolling pullout
Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]] [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]
A hard pull can stall the wing far above the book stall speed
For older airplanes, VA is about 1.7 times the normal stall speed; VA gives no protection against full inputs in more than one axis [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]
Rolling and pulling hard together is not protected even below VA
A spiral may reach or pass VNE; inputs must be slow and gentle [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Raise the nose gently after wings level

body.p: **Control input errors that induce attitudes (R3).** The startled pilot's abrupt muscular effort is hazardous in turbulence, at excessive speeds or at low altitudes [[24:109|AFH 5-4]]. Pulling in a nose-low bank, pushing too far in a nose-high recovery, and an abrupt return to the flightpath that invites a secondary stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] all come from the same root: big inputs without a cross-check.

callout.text: With anyone aboard other than a crewmember, no intentional maneuver may exceed 60° of bank or 30° nose up or down unless every occupant wears an approved parachute. This does not apply to flight tests, or to required maneuvers given by a CFI [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(c), (d)]].

check.q: Why is "I stayed below VA" not a full defense for a recovery made with a hard roll and pull together?
check.a: Operating at or below VA gives no structural protection against full control inputs in more than one axis at the same time [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

chunks.title: Automation: a prevention tool and a trap

body.p: K4 says "if applicable." In a trainer with an autopilot, it is applicable on every flight. Teach both sides.

bullets: **Prevention.** Using the autopilot reduces workload, gives more time to monitor, and lowers the chance of entering an unusual attitude [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. The RMH advises using automation to manage workload, not to make up for a lack of proficiency [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

**Trap.** An autopilot compensating for ice can exceed its limits and disconnect, leaving the airplane in an undesired state with a pilot no longer used to hand flying [[30:51|RMH 7-2]]. Autoflight malfunction can mask the cause of an upset [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].
**Recovery.** Disconnect the wing leveler or autopilot first; manual control is essential, and leaving it on can make control or trim changes that are hard to notice [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

**Exception in the IFH example glass airplane:** with AHRS and air data both failed, the manufacturer recommends turning on the autopilot's roll mode, a wing leveler fed by its own turn coordinator [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

body.p: **Mode awareness.** A change or loss of navigation source may drop the autopilot to wings level mode without the pilot expecting it, which can lead to an undesired aircraft state [[30:52|RMH 7-3]]. Teach anticipate, act, verify, and have the learner read the flight mode annunciators aloud after every button push [[30:51|RMH 7-2]] [[30:52|RMH 7-3]]. One of the most common errors is failing to move to a lower level of automation when things change [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

**Newer systems.** An Emergency Autoland (EAL) system that senses erratic flying stabilizes the airplane and checks for pilot response; with no further input it starts an emergency descent. A pilot or a passenger can also activate it by hand [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]. Application: where one is installed, cover it during the learner's POH/AFM systems study.

check.q: Your learner recovers from an upset with the autopilot still engaged. What does the AFH say?
check.a: Disconnect the wing leveler or autopilot first; manual control is essential, and leaving it on may cause control or trim changes that are hard to recognize [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

chunks.title: Getting back to VMC after inadvertent IMC

body.p: K3 is the reason a private pilot learns this Task. AI.XI.A teaches the full emergency technique (trim, fingertip control, 10° banks, one bar width). Here, focus on what connects it to unusual attitudes: a VFR pilot who loses the horizon is most likely to end up in one.

bullets: **Recognize it.** If a VFR pilot cannot keep attitude control by the natural horizon, it is IMC whatever the weather report says, and a genuine emergency [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

**Keep control first.** The first steps are recognition and acceptance, keeping control, and getting help to land [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. Wings level is the most important concern at first [[24:367|AFH 18-18]]. If the airplane is already in an unusual attitude, recover with the IFH sequence before anything else.
**Ask for help early.** Doubt about weather already puts the airplane in at least an urgency condition; that is the time to ask [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

**Choose VFR over IFR.** A noninstrument-rated pilot should take a course to a safe landing in VFR conditions over a vector into IFR conditions; if VFR cannot be kept, tell the controller, state the lack of an instrument rating and declare distress [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].

**Transition back.** After breaking out, take time to get acclimatized and oriented before an approach, even flying straight and level or circling the airport for a while, especially at night [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

body.p: **Last resort.** The AFH lists emergency response systems right after inadvertent IMC. Where a ballistic parachute is installed, an actual loss of control is one condition that would qualify for deployment. Pilots should know the arming and disarming procedures and the conditions for deployment, and brief passengers who can reach the handle on those conditions and the basic steps [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

callout.text: The AIH warns that introducing flight instruments does not prepare a learner for marginal weather or IMC [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Say it at the end of every hood lesson so a few good recoveries do not become a reason to press on.

check.q: What three first steps does the AFH give a VFR pilot who has entered IMC?
check.a: Recognize and accept how serious it is, keep control of the airplane, and get the help needed to land safely [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

body.p: You are the safety pilot, the traffic scan and the person who puts the airplane in a strange attitude on purpose. Plan the flight around that.

head: Item
What to do
rows: Who may sit right seat

Simulated instrument flight needs a safety pilot with at least a private pilot certificate for the category and class, with adequate vision forward and to each side [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]] [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]]. In its section on night flight training, the AFH adds that practicing unusual attitude recoveries at night should only be done with a flight instructor [[24:224|AFH 11-7]]
Weather
Good enough to make up for the safety pilot's restricted view, with more margin near busy airways or airports [[33:258|AIM 4-3-16]]
Area and traffic

Clear the area with clearing turns before the maneuver [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. The IFH setup for stall practice also fits here: safe altitude, an area free of conflicting traffic, suitable weather, radar traffic advisories [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Altitude

The sources give no altitude for unusual attitude practice. For all maneuvers with significant changes in altitude or direction, the AFH says to make sure the area is clear at and below your altitude and that there is sufficient altitude for a recovery [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Application only, not an FAA number for this Task: some instructors borrow the AFH stall-practice floor (recovery no lower than 1,500 feet AGL in a single-engine airplane) [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] and add the altitude their recoveries in that airplane actually use
Attitude size

The AFH training example is 30° of bank and 15° nose up [[24:107|AFH 5-2]], inside the 91.307(c) limits [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(c), (d)]]; stay within your airplane's approved maneuvers [[24:112|AFH 5-7]]

body.p: **The setup itself.** Brief the plan on the ground, including how the controls will be exchanged [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. No source gives a step-by-step setup script for this Task, so the rest is built from related sources. In unusual attitude training the pilot is often told to close their eyes [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. The IFH and PHAK disorientation demonstrations use eyes closed or the gaze lowered to the floor [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]], and show that a slowly entered, well coordinated turn feels like a climb [[23:75|IFH 3-8]]. Application: take the controls with a positive exchange, maneuver with slow, coordinated changes so the learner cannot follow the attitude by feel, stop in the training attitude and say "recover, you have the flight controls." The IFH ends its learner-flown disorientation demonstration the same way: the instructor tells the pilot to look up and recover [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].

callout.text: Collision hazards (R4): AC 90-48E warns that instructors and safety pilots tend to look inside too much during simulated instrument flight and forget see-and-avoid [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]]. While the learner's head is down and you are maneuvering, your eyes belong outside. Watch the panel only after you hand over.

body.p: **SRM and CRM (S2).** A crew should communicate and confirm the situation clearly and concisely, transfer control to the most situationally aware pilot, and use standardized interactions to manage stress [[24:111|AFH 5-6]]. With you aboard, that is the learner calling "nose low, power, bank, pitch" and you ready to take the controls.

check.q: Which three things does the AFH say a crew should do in an upset, and what do they look like with you and a learner aboard?
check.a: Communicate and confirm the situation clearly and concisely, transfer control to the most situationally aware pilot, and use standardized interactions to manage stress [[24:111|AFH 5-6]]. With a learner, that is clear callouts and a positive exchange of controls.

body.p: **On the ground.** Review the instrument indications and the two sequences until the learner can say them without notes. The AIH advice for anxious learners fits here: tell them what to expect and what the sensations will be, and treat fear as normal [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. UPRT works best when it is conveyed accurately and in a non-threatening manner, through positive experiences [[24:110|AFH 5-5]].

bullets: **Flight 1, eyes open.** Demonstrate a nose-high and a nose-low recovery from the right seat while saying each step, then have the learner follow along on the controls, then have the learner fly one while you follow along [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
**Flight 1, eyes closed.** Set up mild attitudes and say "recover." Grade the assessment out loud before the first input.
**Later flights, partial panel.** Cover the attitude and heading indicators and repeat [[23:162|IFH 7-1]].

**Later flights, distraction.** Let the attitude develop while the learner does a realistic task such as reading a chart or resetting the clock [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. This adds the surprise that eyes-closed drills remove [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].

body.p: **Scenario, not aerobatics.** UPRT differs from aerobatic training: in aerobatics the pilot knows and expects the maneuver, so startle is missing [[24:110|AFH 5-5]]. Scenario-based training with realistic distractions, carrying enough perceived risk to raise stress, is what prepares a pilot for a real upset [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

**Know your own limits.** Airplane-based UPRT is limited by the maneuvers approved for the airplane and by the instructor's own UPRT capabilities [[24:112|AFH 5-7]]. Improper delivery of stall, spin and upset training often results in negative learning [[24:113|AFH 5-8]]. Skills like these are perishable and need continuous reinforcement [[24:110|AFH 5-5]].

callout.text: End each recovery with a one-line debrief while the picture is fresh: "What did airspeed tell you, and what did you move first?" It checks assessment and sequence in one question.

check.q: Why move from eyes-closed setups to attitudes that develop during a distraction task?
check.a: Eyes-closed training removes the element of surprise [[24:107|AFH 5-2]], and real upsets bring surprise and startle; realistic distractions help provoke it in a controlled way [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

body.p: The IFH and AFH lists are short. Each error has a visible sign you can watch for from the right seat.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Not keeping the airplane trimmed [[23:189|IFH 7-28]] [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]
Pressure held on the yoke; the attitude wanders the moment the learner looks away
Trim off every pressure before any flight deck task
Disorganized flight deck [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Hunting for charts or a tablet, head down for long stretches
Arrange items for the flight before takeoff; brief what lives where [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]
Slow cross-check and fixation [[23:189|IFH 7-28]] [[23:221|IFH 7-60]]
Eyes stop on one odd needle; no input for several seconds
Cross-check several instruments for corroboration rather than one [[23:221|IFH 7-60]]; drill recognition on the ground with the IFH figures
Recovering by sensations, not sight [[23:190|IFH 7-29]]
Inputs that match what the learner feels, against the instruments
Disorientation demonstrations, then "trust the instruments" [[23:76|IFH 3-9]]
Weak basic instrument skills [[23:190|IFH 7-29]]
Every basic scan and control error gets bigger in the recovery
Back to straight-and-level, climbs, descents and turns before more recoveries
Incorrect assessment of the upset [[24:112|AFH 5-7]]
Forward pressure with airspeed already high, or power added in a dive
Make the learner name the attitude from airspeed before moving
Not disconnecting the wing leveler or autopilot [[24:112|AFH 5-7]]
Fighting the controls; trim moving on its own
Disconnect is the first action when equipped [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
Not unloading when needed [[24:112|AFH 5-7]]
Back pressure held through the roll-out
Push to about +1 G before rolling level in a spiral [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Rolling the wrong way [[24:112|AFH 5-7]]
Bank increases after the first aileron input
Roll to the nearest horizon [[24:111|AFH 5-6]]; on glass, follow the roll index [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]
Mismanaging airspeed [[24:112|AFH 5-7]]
Power left in during a nose-low recovery, or a stall in a nose-high one
Power is step one in both IFH sequences, in opposite directions [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Overcontrolling after the first input [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Needles reverse and keep going: nose-low becomes nose-high
Fast cross-check after the first input; ease off as the needles slow

callout.text: Read, name, then move: airspeed tells the direction, the turn coordinator tells the bank, and only then do the hands move.

check.q: Your learner fixes a nose-low attitude and ends up with the VSI pegged in a climb. Which error is this and what is the fix?
check.a: Overcontrolling: after the first large input, keep a fast cross-check and relax pressure as the needles slow, since stopping and reversing means passing through level [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

scenario.title: First unusual attitude lesson, glass trainer, hazy afternoon
scenario.setup: You are a new CFI giving a commercial pilot learner her first unusual attitude lesson in a glass-panel trainer with a two-axis autopilot. The practice area floor is 1,200 feet MSL, the haze limits visibility to about 5 miles, and a Victor airway crosses the area. She slept poorly and admits she is nervous because a friend told her these recoveries are "like aerobatics."

questions.q: On the ground, how do you deal with her nerves about "aerobatics"?
questions.a: Treat the fear as normal and describe exactly what she will feel and do [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. Explain that UPRT is not aerobatic training; its goal is safe recovery from unplanned attitudes, not precision maneuvering [[24:110|AFH 5-5]].

questions.q: Does her poor sleep matter for this lesson?
questions.a: Yes. Fatigue and sleep loss increase susceptibility to spatial disorientation [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[23:76|IFH 3-9]], and that is the very thing the lesson stresses. Application: a ground session today is a fair choice.

questions.q: On a rested day with the same haze and airway, what extra care does the setup need?
questions.a: Weather good enough to make up for the safety pilot's restricted view, with more margin near busy airways [[33:258|AIM 4-3-16]], clearing turns before each setup [[24:33|AFH 1-12]], and your eyes outside while she is head down [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]].

questions.q: You say "recover." She opens her eyes, sees red chevrons pointing down on the PFD and pushes hard. What do you watch for?
questions.a: Down-pointing chevrons mean nose-high [[23:217|IFH 7-56]], so a push is right, but the IFH puts power first and the push only to lower the nose and prevent a stall [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. A hard push risks overcontrolling into a nose-low attitude [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

questions.q: On the next setup she rolls further into the bank. What error is it and how do you respond?
questions.a: Rolling the wrong way, an AFH common error [[24:112|AFH 5-7]]. Take the controls if needed, then have her find the bank on the attitude display and the turn rate before moving; above 60° the roll index shows the shortest way to wings level [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

questions.q: She asks whether she can just engage the autopilot next time. What do you teach?
questions.a: The autopilot reduces workload and the chance of entering an unusual attitude [[23:219|IFH 7-58]], but in a recovery the first step is to disconnect it and fly by hand [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Automation is for managing workload, not for covering a lack of proficiency [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

skills.do: Demonstrate and explain, from the right seat, "proper instrument cross-check and interpretation to identify an unusual attitude (including both nose-high and nose-low) in flight, and apply the appropriate flight control, power input, and aircraft configuration in the correct sequence, to return to a stabilized level flight attitude" (ACS AI.XI.E.S1). The ACS gives no numeric tolerance; the examiner looks for a correct assessment, the correct sequence and a stabilized level attitude.
skills.practice: With another applicant as safety pilot, recover from attitudes they set up while you say each step aloud in IFH order [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]], then repeat with the attitude and heading indicators covered [[23:162|IFH 7-1]].

skills.do: "Use single-pilot resource management (SRM) or crew resource management (CRM), as appropriate" (ACS AI.XI.E.S2). The examiner sees you brief the exchange of controls, communicate and confirm the attitude clearly, transfer control to the most aware pilot, and keep the traffic scan going while the learner is head down.
skills.practice: Script your briefing and the "recover, you have the flight controls" handoff [[25:178|AIH 9-8]], and practice clearing turns and outside scanning during the setup [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]].

skills.do: "Analyze and correct common errors related to this Task" (ACS AI.XI.E.S3). When the examiner, playing the learner, pulls in a nose-low bank, rolls the wrong way or fixates, name the error, explain its cause and give the fix.
skills.practice: Learn the IFH and AFH error lists with a "what you see" and a fix for each [[23:189|IFH 7-28]] [[23:190|IFH 7-29]] [[24:112|AFH 5-7]], and take turns flying them for another applicant.

quiz.q: Which part of 14 CFR 61.109(a) puts recovery from unusual flight attitudes into every private pilot applicant's training?
options: The instrument training hours in 61.109(a)(3)
The checkride preparation hours in 61.109(a)(4)
The night training hours in 61.109(a)(2)
The solo flight hours in 61.109(a)(5)
quiz.why: 61.109(a)(3) requires 3 hours on control and maneuvering solely by reference to instruments, including recovery from unusual flight attitudes [[60:300|14 CFR 61.109(a)(3)]].

quiz.q: Per the AFH, under which conditions should UPRT in the airplane be conducted?
options: Only in simulated instrument conditions, under a view-limiting device
In both visual and simulated instrument conditions
Only in visual conditions, so the learner can see the horizon
Only in a full flight simulator, never in the airplane itself
quiz.why: UPRT in the airplane and in flight simulation training devices should be conducted in both visual and simulated instrument conditions, so pilots practice recognition and recovery in both [[24:110|AFH 5-5]].

quiz.q: What does the AFH say limits the upset training a typical flight instructor can give in a normal category trainer?
options: Only the airplane's age and the type of attitude indicator installed
The maneuvers approved for the airplane and the instructor's own UPRT skill
Only the instructor's total flight time and the learner's certificate level
The weather minimums and the airspace class of the practice area
quiz.why: Airplane-based UPRT may be limited by the maneuvers approved for the airplane and by the flight instructor's own UPRT capabilities [[24:112|AFH 5-7]].

quiz.q: On a glass attitude display, the horizon line has started to move downward so brown stays in view. About what pitch has the airplane passed?
options: About 27° nose-down
About 30° nose-up
About 47° nose-up
About 15° nose-down
quiz.why: The horizon line starts moving downward at about 47° nose-up, keeping the brown segment visible; it moves upward at about 27° nose-down [[23:216|IFH 7-55]].

quiz.q: In the IFH nose-high recovery, how much power does the pilot add?
options: Only enough to hold the entry altitude
None until the wings are level again
Full power every time, whatever the airspeed
In proportion to the observed deceleration
quiz.why: Increase power as necessary in proportion to the observed deceleration [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].

quiz.q: During initial training, how does the IFH want a learner to make a nose-low recovery?
options: All three controls blended smoothly at once from the first lesson
Using the attitude indicator alone and ignoring the other gauges
In whatever order of controls feels most natural to the learner
By the numbers, one step after another in the order given
quiz.why: All controls can be changed at once in a smooth, proficient recovery, but in initial training a positive, confident recovery should be made by the numbers, in the sequence given [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

quiz.q: After an AHRS failure in the IFH example glass airplane, which coordination aid is left for the recovery?
options: The slip/skid indicator on the standby attitude indicator
A standby turn coordinator below the PFD
None; no slip/skid display or standby turn coordinator
The autopilot's turn coordinator, shown on the MFD
quiz.why: The slip/skid indicator is no longer present and no standby turn coordinator is installed [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]; the autopilot's turn coordinator sits behind the MFD where the pilot cannot use it [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

quiz.q: Your private pilot learner wants to practice unusual attitude recoveries at night with a pilot friend as safety pilot. What does the AFH say?
options: It is fine as long as all the flight deck lights stay on
It should be practiced only with a flight instructor aboard
It is best done on nights with a bright moon and clear skies
It is fine if the friend holds at least a private pilot certificate
quiz.why: In its night flight training section, the AFH says practicing recovery from unusual attitudes should only be done with a flight instructor [[24:224|AFH 11-7]].

quiz.q: What does the RMH say can happen when an autopilot compensating for ice accumulation exceeds its limits?
options: It holds altitude and sounds a warning
It reverts to heading mode and stays fully engaged
It may disconnect and leave an undesired state
It levels the wings and hands over trimmed
quiz.why: The system could disconnect and leave the aircraft in an undesired state, with a pilot unaccustomed to manual flight [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

quiz.q: In an airplane with an Emergency Autoland (EAL) system, what does the AFH say the system does when it senses erratic flying?
options: Reduces power to idle and starts a spiral descent
Stabilizes the airplane and checks for pilot response
Disconnects the autopilot and sounds a warning tone
Deploys the ballistic parachute after 25 seconds
quiz.why: If the EAL senses erratic flying, it stabilizes the aircraft and checks for pilot responsiveness; without further input it starts an emergency descent [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner is reading a chart when turbulence drops a wing about 10°. She sees it at once and stops it with a small, matching aileron input before the bank grows. What does the AFH call this kind of prevention?
options: Following the upset recovery template
Proportional counter-response
Unloading the wing before rolling level
A positive exchange of flight controls
final_quiz.why: Proportional counter-response is the timely use of flight controls and thrust to manage an unintended excursion, recognizing a developing upset and taking proportionally appropriate action before it becomes fully developed [[24:111|AFH 5-6]].

final_quiz.q: After you say "recover," your learner applies aileron that steepens the existing left bank. Which AFH common error is this?
options: Failure to roll in the correct direction
Mismanaging the airspeed
Failure to disconnect the wing leveler first
Failure to unload the airplane
final_quiz.why: Failure to roll in the correct direction is on the AFH list of upset recovery errors [[24:112|AFH 5-7]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner is new to the glass trainer and wants to hand fly every simulated instrument flight with the autopilot off. What does the IFH say flying an EFD airplane without the autopilot has been shown to do for pilots first learning the system?
options: Increase workload and decrease situational awareness
Make an AHRS failure easier for the pilot to spot
Make no difference once the pilot is instrument rated
Build hand flying skill faster with no added risk
final_quiz.why: Flying an EFD-equipped aircraft without the autopilot has been shown to increase workload and decrease situational awareness for pilots first learning the system; the autopilot reduces workload and the chance of entering an unusual attitude [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. Balance it with hand flying practice, since automation should manage workload, not cover a lack of proficiency [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot's vacuum pump fails in VMC with IMC ahead, and he continues. Analyzed with PAVE as the AIH does, what made the risk unacceptable?
options: A pilot hazard and an external pressure, with no aircraft hazard
An environment hazard alone, from the IMC
An aircraft hazard combined with an environment hazard
An external pressure combined with a pilot hazard
final_quiz.why: The failed instruments were an aircraft hazard and IMC an environment hazard; the combination created an unacceptable risk [[25:186|AIH 10-2]].

final_quiz.q: Your trainer's attitude indicator shows pitch only to plus or minus 25°. You plan a 35° nose-up setup for an advanced learner. What does the PHAK warn the instrument may do?
options: Show the right pitch, but a few seconds late
Flag itself as failed, then realign itself within a minute
Peg at its limit, or tumble and show false pitch and bank
Show correct bank while the pitch bars go blank
final_quiz.why: An attitude indicator that displays pitch only to plus or minus 25° could peg at that indication, or tumble and give erroneous pitch and bank, which can confuse a pilot during an unusual attitude recovery [[1:221|PHAK 8-19]].

final_quiz.q: A navigation source change drops your learner's autopilot into wings level mode and she does not notice. Which habit from the RMH addresses this?
options: Leave flight path monitoring to ATC radar
Never engage the autopilot at all during instrument training
Engage altitude hold before every heading change
Anticipate, act and verify, reading the mode annunciators
final_quiz.why: A change of navigation source may drop the autopilot to wings level mode; understanding the system lets the pilot anticipate, act and verify [[30:52|RMH 7-3]] [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

final_quiz.q: An advanced learner asks for upset recoveries from beyond 90° of bank in your normal category trainer. What does the AFH say training like that needs?
options: A suitable airplane or simulator and a qualified instructor
Only an extra briefing and a second safety pilot aboard
Only the learner's written consent and a logbook entry
Nothing extra if the learner holds an instrument rating
final_quiz.why: Recovery from bank angles beyond 90° needs extra measures to make sure the airplane or simulator is suitable and the instructors are appropriately qualified [[24:110|AFH 5-5]]; airplane-based UPRT is limited by the maneuvers approved for the airplane [[24:112|AFH 5-7]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner leaves her first unusual attitude lesson shaken and says she never wants to try it again. Which AFH UPRT core concept did the lesson most likely miss?
options: Practice only in a full flight simulator before using an airplane
Keep her eyes closed so no attitude can ever surprise her
Show bank angles past 90° early so later ones feel mild
Convey it accurately, without threat, through positive experiences
final_quiz.why: UPRT concepts should be conveyed accurately and in a non-threatening manner; positive experiences improve understanding, retention and the desire for more training [[24:110|AFH 5-5]].

final_quiz.q: Your VFR learner breaks out below a cloud layer about 1,200 feet over unfamiliar terrain at dusk and wants to land at once. What does the AFH advise?
options: Land at the nearest field before dark
Ask ATC for a no-gyro approach to any airport
Take time to get oriented, even circling for a while
Climb back into the cloud to stay above terrain
final_quiz.why: Allow time to become acclimatized and geographically oriented before an approach, even if it means flying straight and level or circling, especially at night [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

final_quiz.q: Your instrument student aces every eyes-closed recovery. To protect her against startle in a real upset, what does the AFH say the training scenarios need?
options: Bank angles past 90° on every lesson
More eyes-closed setups at higher altitude
Aerobatic entries that she has fully briefed in advance
Enough perceived risk to raise her stress level
final_quiz.why: Scenario-based training with realistic distractions protects against startle, and the scenarios should carry a perception of risk sufficient to elevate stress [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's nose-low recoveries are quick, but each ends with the VSI swinging from 1,500 fpm down to 1,000 fpm up. What does the IFH tell her to do?
options: Make all three inputs at once from the start
Watch only the attitude indicator during the recovery
Hold back pressure until the VSI reads zero
Keep a fast cross-check after the first big input
final_quiz.why: After initial control is applied, continue a fast cross-check for overcontrolling, since the first pressures may be large; stopping and reversing needles mean passing through level [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

final_quiz.q: On your CFI checkride the examiner asks for a nose-low recovery. Which describes the standard in AI.XI.E.S1?
options: Identify it by cross-check, then use controls, power and configuration in sequence to stable level flight
Return to the entry altitude within 100 feet and to the entry heading within 10° before leveling the wings
Recover using only the attitude indicator, with every input complete within 5 seconds of the call
Recover with the autopilot engaged in roll mode, then explain each step to the examiner afterward
final_quiz.why: S1 requires cross-check and interpretation to identify the attitude, then flight control, power and configuration in the correct sequence to a stabilized level flight attitude (ACS AI.XI.E.S1). The IFH nose-low order is power, bank, pitch [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner arrives after a red-eye trip with a cold and has taken an antihistamine. Which IFH point bears most directly on today's unusual attitude lesson?
options: Illness, medication and sleep loss raise disorientation risk
Spillable gyros can tumble in steep attitudes and mislead her
Turbulence is the leading cause of upsets
Partial panel work needs a vacuum gauge
final_quiz.why: Illness, medication, fatigue and sleep loss are likely to increase susceptibility to spatial disorientation [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

takeaways: Read, name, then move: airspeed tells nose-high or nose-low before any input.
Nose-high: power up, push, level the wings. Nose-low: power down, level the wings, then raise the nose.
Teach recoveries on partial panel too; the IFH sequence starts from the airspeed indicator, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator.
Prevention has four doors: flight causal, physiological, environmental, and system and equipment failures.
Set up safely: brief, clear, enough altitude, eyes outside while the learner is head down, a clear "recover" handoff.
Eyes-closed drills teach the sequence; distraction scenarios add the surprise real upsets bring.
Disconnect the autopilot to recover, but use automation to keep workload low and avoid upsets.
cfi_notes: The IFH and AFH give different orders. The IFH nose-high recovery is power, pitch, bank and nose-low is power, bank, pitch [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]; the AFH upset template is disconnect, unload, roll, power, return [[24:111|AFH 5-6]], and both defer to the POH/AFM. Pick one per learner, name its source, and do not mix them mid-lesson.

The AFH stall recovery puts AOA reduction before power [[24:121|AFH 5-16]], while the IFH nose-high recovery puts power first [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. They fit different pictures: nose-high with airspeed decaying versus an airplane already showing stall cues. Teach the learner to decide from airspeed and stall indications.

No source gives a minimum altitude for unusual attitude practice; the AFH only asks for a clear area and sufficient altitude for a recovery [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. If you borrow the AFH 1,500 feet AGL stall-practice floor [[24:121|AFH 5-16]], present it as your own standard, and do not quiz learners on it as an FAA number.

The AFH notes that eyes-closed training removes surprise [[24:107|AFH 5-2]], yet the IFH and PHAK build their disorientation demonstrations on closed eyes [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]]. Use both: eyes closed for sequence and disorientation, distraction scenarios for startle.

Attitude indicator tumble limits differ by model; the PHAK gives 100° to 110° of bank and 60° to 70° of pitch for some, and notes that some only show plus or minus 25° of pitch and can peg [[1:221|PHAK 8-19]]. Know the gyro in your airplane before you set up steep attitudes.

The AIH distraction list (drop a pencil, reset the clock, read a chart) is written mainly for stall training, though its opening line names upsets too [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. It transfers well to unusual attitudes, but give head-turning tasks with care because of the Coriolis illusion [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].

14 CFR 91.307(d)(2) exempts required maneuvers given by a CFI from the parachute rule [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(c), (d)]], but the AFH training example of 30° bank and 15° nose up [[24:107|AFH 5-2]] fits inside the limits anyway. Larger attitudes add little for a normal category trainer.

Bank angles beyond 90° add to upset training only with a suitable airplane or simulator and appropriately qualified instructors [[24:110|AFH 5-5]]. That is a referral, not something to try in a trainer.

No source gives a setup script for unusual attitudes. The eyes-closed setup in this lesson is pieced together from the AFH remark that pilots are often told to close their eyes [[24:107|AFH 5-2]], the IFH and PHAK disorientation demonstrations [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]] and the AIH control exchange [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]; the "recover" handoff is application.
gaps: The POH/AFM unusual attitude or upset procedure, if your airplane has one, overrides the IFH order; most trainer POHs must be checked individually.
No source gives a minimum altitude, a maximum training bank or pitch, or a set number of setups for an unusual attitude lesson.
The sources do not describe how to fit or remove a view-limiting device during an unusual attitude setup, or how to handle a learner who removes it mid-recovery.
No source states how much altitude a typical trainer loses in a nose-low recovery; measure it in your airplane and use that number in your planning.
The IFH glass panel numbers (chevrons at 30° nose-up and 15° nose-down, roll index past 60°) describe one example system [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]; check the avionics manual for your PFD.

activities.title: True or false: recovering with less than a full panel
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Except for the instrument takeoff, the IFH analog maneuvers can all be flown with the attitude and heading indicators covered.
With no POH/AFM procedure, the IFH starts the recovery from the airspeed indicator, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator.
On partial panel, the altimeter is the primary pitch reference for holding altitude.
cards.why: True. Partial panel practice uses the altimeter as the primary pitch indicator [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].

cards.s: In the IFH example glass airplane, the analog standby attitude indicator stays usable in any pitch or bank.
cards.why: False. In extreme nose-high or nose-low attitudes and high bank angles it can tumble and become unusable [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

cards.s: On partial panel, a quick, large yoke input to an altitude error stops the oscillation sooner.
cards.why: False. Rapid control movements compound the deviation with an oscillation; first stop the needle with a smooth input [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].

cards.s: Covering a failed instrument may help the pilot keep control.

activities.title: Envelope and recovery numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Recovering on a PFD, the airspeed trend vector points 18 knots below the current airspeed. About how many knots per second is the airspeed falling?
items.why: Trend vectors show where airspeed will be in 6 seconds [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]: 18 / 6 = 3 knots per second. Falling airspeed means nose-high, so power comes up first [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].

items.q: Nose-low, the VSI shows 2,400 fpm down, and your learner stares at the altimeter for 5 seconds before her first input. About how many feet does she lose while staring?
items.why: 2,400 fpm / 60 = 40 feet per second x 5 seconds = 200 feet. The impulse to stop and stare at a discrepancy is the IFH slow cross-check and fixation error [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

items.q: Your setup ends at 32° of bank and 18° nose up. How many more degrees of nose-up pitch could it gain and still stay inside the AFH upset pitch parameter?
items.why: An upset includes pitch greater than 25° nose up [[24:106|AFH 5-1]]: 25 - 18 = 7 degrees. The 32° bank is also inside the 45° bank parameter, so this is an unusual attitude, not an upset.

items.q: After a recovery your learner is 350 feet below the assigned altitude. Using the IFH double-the-error rule, above what vertical speed is she overcontrolling?
items.why: Rate wanted: 2 x 350 = 700 fpm, inside the 500 to 1,000 fpm optimum [[23:197|IFH 7-36]] [[23:198|IFH 7-37]]. More than 200 fpm over the wanted rate is overcontrolling: 700 + 200 = 900 fpm [[23:198|IFH 7-37]].

activities.title: Setting up an unusual attitude, in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the instructor's steps in order, then tap Check. (No source gives one script; this order is built from AIH 9-8, AFH 5-16, AFH 1-12, IFH 3-8 and IFH 7-28.)
steps: On the ground, brief the plan, the "recover" call and how controls will be exchanged
Clear the area at and below you, with enough altitude for a recovery
Take the controls with a positive three-step exchange
Learner closes eyes while you maneuver slowly, your eyes outside
Stop in the training attitude and say "recover, you have the flight controls"
Learner cross-checks, names the attitude and recovers in IFH order
Learner returns to the starting altitude, then you debrief

activities.title: Teaching the first recovery, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are teaching a private pilot learner her first unusual attitude recoveries in a six-pack trainer, in good VMC, as instructor and safety pilot.

steps.s: On the ground she asks what she should do first when you say "recover."
options: Read the airspeed and name the attitude
Push the nose down right away to build speed and get out of the attitude
Roll the wings level by feel, without waiting to look at the instruments
Add full power and wait to see where the airplane settles
steps.why: Any odd rate or reading means assume an unusual attitude and speed up the cross-check to confirm it [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]; incorrect assessment is the first AFH error [[24:112|AFH 5-7]].

steps.s: Airborne and level before your first setup. What do you confirm before you take the controls?
options: She already has her eyes closed
The area is clear below you, with room to recover
ATC has approved a block altitude
The autopilot is holding the altitude
steps.why: For all maneuvers with significant changes in altitude or direction, make sure the area is clear of traffic at and below your altitude and that there is sufficient altitude for a recovery [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]; clearing turns do the first part [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

steps.s: She opens her eyes to airspeed rising, a left bank and the altimeter unwinding. She starts to pull. What do you say?
options: "Add power to hold altitude while the bank comes out"
"Pull harder, the nose is low and the airspeed is rising"
"Roll right and pull together to recover quickly"
"Power off, wings level, then ease back"
steps.why: Nose-low order: reduce power, level the wings, then raise the nose with smooth back pressure; the pull is the instinctive wrong reaction [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

steps.s: You set that one up from 4,500 feet. She recovers to stable, straight-and-level flight at 4,150 feet and starts to trim for cruise there. What do you coach?
options: Nothing, the recovery ended once she was level
Descend to 4,000 for an even altitude
Climb back to 4,500 now that she is stable
Climb back while still rolling the wings level
steps.why: When the unusual attitude was entered from an assigned altitude, whether set by an instructor or by ATC, the IFH says to return to it after stabilizing in straight-and-level flight [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

steps.s: In the debrief she says she now feels ready to handle a cloud on her cross-country. How do you respond?
options: Agree, since her recoveries met the standard for this lesson
Say she is ready if she keeps the autopilot on the whole time
Tell her to avoid only thunderstorms and nothing else
Explain this training is not preparation for IMC
steps.why: Learners must understand that the introduction to flight instruments does not prepare them for marginal weather or IMC [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].
